features.doc: The second utterance of a sequence.
Whether the context lets the second utterance revise the first.
The form of an utterance challenged as a lie or disbelieved.

examples.primaryText: Stand at attention!
examples.comment: Group I: speaker desire and addressee inducement both present. Described afterwards as: He ordered me to stand at attention.

examples.primaryText: Don't touch the hot plate!
examples.comment: Described afterwards as: He warned me not to touch the hot plate.

examples.primaryText: Hand me the salt, please.
examples.comment: Described afterwards as: He requested to be passed the salt.

examples.primaryText: Take these pills for a week.
examples.comment: Advice with a salient shared goal falls in Group I. Described afterwards as: He advised me to take the pills for a week.

examples.primaryText: Please, lend me the money!
examples.comment: Described afterwards as: He pleaded with me to lend him the money.

examples.primaryText: Get well soon!
examples.comment: Group II: the addressee is taken to have no control over the content; no inducement to act. Described afterwards as: He wished me to get well soon.

examples.primaryText: Drop dead!
examples.comment: Described afterwards as: He cursed me to drop dead.

examples.primaryText: Please, don't rain!
examples.comment: Described afterwards as: He expressed the wish that it not rain. The paper prints the use label as 'addresee-less wish'.

examples.primaryText: Be blond!
examples.context: On the way to a blind date.
examples.comment: Described afterwards as: He wished for his date to be blond.

examples.primaryText: Okay, go out and play.
examples.comment: Group III: neither speaker desire nor inducement; any enticement to act comes from a pre-existing addressee desire. Described afterwards as: He allowed me to go out and play.

examples.primaryText: Have a cookie, if you like.
examples.comment: The paper brackets the conditional clause; offers without it are treated as implicitly conditionalized preferences. Described afterwards as: He offered me a cookie.

examples.primaryText: Come to dinner tonight, if you like.
examples.comment: The paper prints 'Come to dinner tonight(, if you like).'; this row is the variant with the conditional clause. Described afterwards as: He invited me to go to dinner that night.

examples.primaryText: Take the train that leaves from over there in 10 minutes.
discourseSegments: A: Excuse me, how do I get to San Francisco?
B: Take the train that leaves from over there in 10 minutes.
examples.context: Strangers in the streets of Palo Alto; B points to the train station.
examples.comment: Group IV: the speaker has no interest in the fulfilment of the imperative; the addressee's motivation derives from a prior goal.

examples.primaryText: Be at the airport at noon!
examples.comment: The imperative can never be described with the paired declarative, a promise: He promised me that I will/would be at the airport at noon.

examples.primaryText: Stay out of trouble!
examples.comment: The imperative can never be described with the paired declarative, a claim: He claimed that I (would/will) stay out of trouble.

examples.primaryText: Take the Northbound train to go to San Francisco!
examples.comment: The paper prints 'Take the Northbound train (to go to San Francisco)!'; this row is the variant with the purpose clause. The imperative can never be described with the paired declarative, a claim: He claimed that I will take the Northbound train (to go to San Francisco).

examples.primaryText: Stay inside all day! Since you enjoy the nice weather, go out and play a little bit.
discourseSegments: Stay inside all day!
Since you enjoy the nice weather, go out and play a little bit.
examples.comment: Portner's observation that conflicting imperatives are odd even across subtypes, an order and a suggestion, unless the speaker has changed their mind.

examples.primaryText: Stay inside all day! Okay, go outside and play in the afternoon!
discourseSegments: Stay inside all day!
Okay, go outside and play in the afternoon!
examples.comment: A command followed by a permission that limits its scope: the command no longer applies to the afternoon.

examples.primaryText: Okay, go but don't go quite yet!
examples.comment: A permission followed by a request that limits it: the permission is not operative right after the utterance.

examples.primaryText: Okay, stay out late but be sure to be back by 1!
examples.comment: A permission followed by a command that limits it.

examples.primaryText: Please, rain tomorrow so the picnic gets cancelled! Please, don't rain tomorrow so I can go hiking!
discourseSegments: Please, rain tomorrow so the picnic gets cancelled!
Please, don't rain tomorrow so I can go hiking!
examples.comment: Two wishes with incompatible contents, incoherent even though they induce no action: it sounds as if the speaker were vacillating. Printed unmarked; the prose says 'contradicting imperatives expressing wishes are incoherent'.

examples.primaryText: I want it to rain tomorrow so the picnic gets cancelled but, on the other hand, I don't want it to rain tomorrow so I can go hiking.
examples.comment: A desiderative assertion of two incompatible desires; underlying desires need not be consistent, only effective preferences must.

examples.primaryText: Call him at home! I don't want you to but he is fine with that.
discourseSegments: Call him at home!
I don't want you to but he is fine with that.
examples.comment: A directive followed by a denial of the speaker's desire; the paper credits the observation to Schwager and Kaufmann.

examples.primaryText: Officially, you are not allowed to but just go through this door.
discourseSegments: A: How do I get into the building?
B: Officially, you are not allowed to but just go through this door.
examples.comment: Disinterested advice with a statement that acting on it is not permitted: a deontic statement is no preference of the speaker against the content.

examples.primaryText: I don't want you to but just go through this door.
discourseSegments: A: How do I get into the building?
B: I don't want you to but just go through this door.
examples.comment: Disinterested advice followed by a denial of the speaker's desire.

examples.primaryText: The only way is through this door. But I don't want you to go through this door.
discourseSegments: A: How do I get into the building?
B: The only way is through this door. But I don't want you to go through this door.

contrasts.form: The only way is through this door. But you are not allowed to go through this door.

examples.comment: The information is given by a declarative, so no preferential commitment is incurred and the denial conflicts with nothing.

examples.primaryText: OK, go to Paris then since you want it so much! But, don't forget, I don't want you to.
discourseSegments: OK, go to Paris then since you want it so much!
But, don't forget, I don't want you to.
examples.comment: A concession followed by a present-tense denial of the speaker's desire.

examples.primaryText: OK, go to Paris then since you want it so much! But, don't forget, I didn't want you to.
discourseSegments: OK, go to Paris then since you want it so much!
But, don't forget, I didn't want you to.
examples.comment: A concession followed by a past-tense report of the speaker's earlier desire, which the concession has overridden.

examples.primaryText: OK, go through this door. But it's officially prohibited so I wish you would not.
discourseSegments: OK, go through this door.
But it's officially prohibited so I wish you would not.
examples.comment: A concession followed by a wish against the content: wish, unlike want, can express a desire the agent takes to be unrealizable, a preference that is not effective.

examples.primaryText: A: I want you to give me an aspirin! B: No, you don't, you are lying.
discourseSegments: A: I want you to give me an aspirin!
B: No, you don't, you are lying.
examples.comment: An assertion of a desire challenged as a lie; the paper credits Schwager, who attributes the example to Manfred Bierwisch.

examples.primaryText: A: Give me an aspirin! B: You are lying, you don't want me to give you one.
discourseSegments: A: Give me an aspirin!
B: You are lying, you don't want me to give you one.
examples.comment: An imperative challenged as a lie.

examples.primaryText: A: I want you to give me an aspirin! B: I don't believe you, you don't really want me to give you one.
discourseSegments: A: I want you to give me an aspirin!
B: I don't believe you, you don't really want me to give you one.
examples.comment: An assertion of a desire met with disbelief.

examples.primaryText: A: Give me an aspirin! B: I don't believe you, you don't really want me to give you one.
discourseSegments: A: Give me an aspirin!
B: I don't believe you, you don't really want me to give you one.
examples.comment: An imperative met with disbelief.

examples.primaryText: A: I order you to administer this drug. B: I don't believe you, you didn't just order me to administer the drug.
discourseSegments: A: I order you to administer this drug.
B: I don't believe you, you didn't just order me to administer the drug.

contrasts.form: A: I order you to administer this drug. B: You are lying, you didn't just order me to administer the drug.

examples.comment: An explicit performative met with disbelief or challenged as a lie; explicit performatives are self-verifying like imperatives.

examples.primaryText: Be at the airport at noon! If necessary, I can give you a ride.
discourseSegments: Be at the airport at noon!
If necessary, I can give you a ride.
examples.comment: The speaker offers a supporting action that enables the addressee: speaker involvement is limited, not excluded.

examples.primaryText: Be in the conference room in three minutes!
examples.context: Uttered in order to get the addressee to sit still so that the speaker can carry them to the conference room.
examples.comment: An imperative cannot merely tell the addressee not to interfere with the speaker's own plan to bring the content about. Printed unmarked; the prose gives it as the 'extreme example' of a use imperatives do not have.

examples.primaryText: Have a good trip and get a lot of work done on the train!
examples.comment: The first conjunct is a well-wish; the second cannot be read as a mere wish, since the addressee controls its content, and rings as an exhortation: the prediction of the two conditions on wish uses.

examples.primaryText: Stand up and walk!
examples.context: Uttered by magicians, gods, and other agents of supernatural powers.
examples.comment: The limiting case in which the utterance suffices to realize the preference it expresses.

examples.primaryText: Rise from the dead, Lazarus!
examples.context: Uttered by magicians, gods, and other agents of supernatural powers.

examples.primaryText: Take a cookie, if you like.
examples.comment: The paper prints 'Take a cookie, if you like (to take a cookie).'; this row omits the parenthesized spell-out of the elided complement. Treated as a reduced conditional expressing a conditional preference: if you want to take a cookie, I want you to take one.

examples.primaryText: Take the train. But you know how dangerous I think this is, so I don't want you to take it.
discourseSegments: A: How will I get to San Francisco?
B: Take the train. But you know how dangerous I think this is, so I don't want you to take it.
examples.comment: Disinterested advice followed by a denial of the speaker's desire; the paper gives the want and wish continuations as one example with a slash.

examples.primaryText: Take the train. But you know how dangerous I think this is, so I wish you would not.
discourseSegments: A: How will I get to San Francisco?
B: Take the train. But you know how dangerous I think this is, so I wish you would not.
examples.comment: Disinterested advice followed by a wish against the content; unlike the concession in (22), advice tolerates no preference of any kind against its content.
